n: Perioperative Care in Obstetrics and Gynaecology

faq.a: It standardises critical steps, reduces omissions, and improves communication, which is vital where staffing and equipment may be limited.
faq.q: Why is the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist important in low‑resource settings?

faq.a: Ensure proper skin preparation with chlorhexidine, give appropriate antibiotics, maintain normothermia, and keep the wound dry and covered.
faq.q: How can I reduce the risk of postoperative wound infection without advanced dressings?

exam: What pre‑operative investigations are essential for a 28‑year‑old HIV‑positive woman scheduled for emergency caesarean? — Identify CBC, renal function, blood group, CD4 count; explain how each influences anaesthetic and antibiotic choices.

A patient develops uterine atony after delivery despite oxytocin infusion. What is your next step and why? — Give a second‑line uterotonic (e.g., methylergometrine) and consider uterine massage; explain contraindications.
How does severe anaemia alter intra‑operative management? — Discuss need for blood transfusion, careful fluid balance, and monitoring of oxygen delivery.

Explain the rationale for using cefazolin prophylaxis and why a macrolide would be avoided in this setting. — Cefazolin covers skin flora; macrolides have poor gram‑positive coverage and risk of QT prolongation.

A woman presents with fever 48 hours after myomectomy. How do you differentiate surgical site infection from malaria? — Review wound appearance, obtain wound swab, perform malaria smear; explain differing treatments.
What are the key components of the WHO checklist that directly impact maternal safety? — Time‑out, antibiotic administration, equipment check, and postoperative count; link each to outcomes.

Describe how you would manage postoperative hypertension in a patient with pre‑eclampsia after a caesarean section. — Use labetalol IV, avoid rapid‑acting nifedipine bolus, monitor urine output and reflexes.
Why is early ambulation emphasized after gynaecologic surgery, and what complications does it prevent? — Reduces venous stasis, lowers risk of DVT and pulmonary embolism, promotes bowel motility.
ai.title: Perioperative Care in Obstetrics and Gynaecology
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Guides safe perioperative management of obstetric and gynaecologic patients in low‑resource settings, focusing on risk assessment, preparation, intra‑operative monitoring, and post‑operative care.

b: Encompasses obstetric (caesarean section, hysterectomy for placenta accreta) and gynaecologic procedures (myomectomy, ovarian cystectomy).
Goal: optimise maternal physiology, prevent infection, control bleeding, and ensure fetal wellbeing when applicable.
sections.p: Perioperative care comprises pre‑operative assessment, intra‑operative management, and post‑operative monitoring to minimise morbidity and mortality around surgery or delivery.

b: ASA I–II: low risk, routine monitoring.
ASA III–IV: high risk, need senior anaesthetist, possible ICU backup.
sections.p: Risk is stratified using the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist and the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status classification.

b: Anaemia (common in malaria, hookworm, chronic blood loss).
Infection (HIV, TB, urinary tract infection, malaria).
Cardiovascular disease (rheumatic heart disease, hypertension).
Malnutrition and electrolyte disturbances.
sections.p: Factors that increase peri‑operative risk in this setting are often related to co‑morbidities and resource limitations.

b: Pre‑op: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, tachycardia, low haemoglobin, uncontrolled hypertension.
Intra‑op: hypotension, tachycardia, excessive bleeding, uterine atony.
Post‑op: fever, wound infection, wound dehiscence, pulmonary embolus, sepsis.
sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic pre‑operatively but present with signs of decompensation intra‑ or post‑operatively.

t.b: Detect anaemia, infection, thrombocytopenia – guides transfusion and antibiotic need.
Identify dehydration, renal impairment – informs fluid management.

t.a: HIV test (rapid) & CD4 count if positive
t.b: Determine need for prophylactic antibiotics and antiretroviral timing.
Assess fetal wellbeing, uterine scar thickness, ovarian mass size – influences surgical plan.
Prepare for possible transfusion; if unavailable, arrange donor or use blood‑saving techniques.

b: Severe hypertension (>160/110 mmHg) or pre‑eclampsia signs.
Rapid drop in oxygen saturation <90% on room air.
Acute renal failure (creatinine rise >2 mg/dL).
Signs of sepsis: temperature >38°C, heart rate >100, white cell count >12 ×10⁹/L.
sections.p: Early recognition of these signs prevents catastrophic outcomes.

b: Pre‑op: correct anaemia (iron, transfusion if severe), treat infections (antibiotics, antimalarials), control BP (hydralazine, labetalol).
Intra‑op: use WHO checklist, give prophylactic cefazolin (or ceftriaxone if cefazolin unavailable), maintain normothermia, monitor pulse, BP, SpO₂, urine output.
Post‑op: analgesia with paracetamol ± NSAID (avoid NSAID if renal impairment), early ambulation, wound care, monitor for bleeding and infection.
Avoid: ketamine in uncontrolled hypertension, NSAIDs in renal failure, high‑dose oxytocin bolus in cardiac disease.
sections.p: A stepwise approach: optimise the patient, prevent complications, treat any arising problem promptly.

b: Schedule review at 1 week and 6 weeks.
Iron supplementation for 3 months if anaemia persists.
Counselling on family planning to avoid repeat high‑risk surgery.
Vaccination updates (HBV, tetanus).
sections.p: Post‑discharge review focuses on wound healing, anaemia correction, and chronic disease control.

b: Post‑operative fever vs. malaria relapse – obtain malaria smear if endemic.
Uterine atony vs. retained placenta – examine uterine tone and perform gentle curettage if needed.
Haemoglobin may be falsely high if sample is haemolysed; repeat if clinical picture suggests anaemia.
Rapid HIV test can give false‑negative in early infection – consider repeat after 4 weeks if risk high.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe chest pain or dyspnoea post‑operatively
High fever with rigors after surgery
